title: Effectiveness of a combined paced-breathing and mobile app–based mindfulness intervention for chronic migraine: A randomized controlled trial
abstract: Background: Mindfulness has been proposed as a non-pharmacological strategy for chronic migraine management. Objective: This study evaluated the effectiveness of a combined paced-breathing and mobile app–based mindfulness intervention in adults with chronic migraine. Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted in adults with chronic migraine. Forty participants were randomized, and 38 were included in the final analyses. The intervention group was assigned to a 12-week combined intervention consisting of paced breathing followed by a mobile app–based mindfulness intervention delivered through the Petit BamBou® app; the control group remained on a waitlist and continued usual care. The primary outcome was migraine days per month. Secondary outcomes included migraine episode pain intensity and duration, headache-related quality of life (Headache Impact Test-6), anxiety sensitivity (Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3), kinesiophobia (Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia-11), and sleep quality (Athens Insomnia Scale). Between-group differences at post-intervention were evaluated using analysis of covariance, adjusting each outcome for its corresponding baseline value. Results: No statistically significant baseline-adjusted between-group differences were observed for migraine frequency or for any secondary outcome. For the primary outcome, the adjusted mean difference between the control and intervention groups was −3.07 migraine days per month (95% CI, −8.00 to 1.86; F(1, 35) = 1.599; p = 0.214; ηp2 = 0.044). Effect sizes were small for all outcomes. Conclusion: A 12-week combined paced-breathing and mobile app–based mindfulness intervention was not superior to waitlist usual care for reducing migraine frequency or improving the evaluated clinical and psychological outcomes. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the small sample size, the marked baseline imbalance in migraine frequency, the use of a waitlist control group, and the absence of objective adherence monitoring. Future trials should include larger samples, active control conditions, objective measures of engagement, and longer follow-up periods. (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, ACTRN12624000611527 [prospectively registered on May 10, 2024]).
